transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Pioneer CTO), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Rachael Ortiz (SRE), Ibrahim Khan, Anna Liu

Summary (auto): quick notes about p99 spikes tied to intermittent kv cache misses and cross-region peering; streaming reduces tail in single-node cases but amplifies network hop variance in VPC peering; quantization reduces per-token latency but may increase variance on cold paths.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll get started, feel free to interrupt. Maya from Redwood, Diego will do the deep runtime bits.
[00:12] Lena Park: Thanks Maya. We wanted to focus on the p95/p99 behaviour we're seeing in our staging cluster, sometimes p99 jumps to 1.2s from a 220ms baseline.
[00:24] Diego Ramirez: OK yeah, that kind of amplification almost always points to either KV cache misses, or network hop variance; curious, do you have a diagram of the VPC mesh?
[00:33] Rachael Ortiz: I put a sketch in the invite but it's rough, we have an on-prem edge that peeks into the cloud over a peering connection, then traffic goes to a host pool in eu-west and then to the GPU nodes. There can be an extra hop when the edge forwards to a failover region.
[00:48] Diego Ramirez: Right, so that extra hop — even if tiny — can blow out the tail because streaming keeps the request open and accumulates jitter. With non-streaming/batched requests, you see more consistent per-token cost but higher median latency.
[01:06] Samir Patel: Wait can you repeat that? We thought streaming always lowered tail.
[01:10] Diego Ramirez: It's nuanced. Streaming reduces median and often p95 for single-hop, local traffic because you emit tokens as they're generated. But if network hops are variable — like 2 extra TCP handshakes or a peering spike — the open stream experiences the entire jitter window and p99 degrades. So streaming amplifies network variance.
[01:34] Lena Park: That matches what we observe: spikes appear correlated with certain flows during backups, like when our storage replication runs.
[01:42] Maya Chen: Two things we'll look at: route by policy (keep critical traffic on low-hop paths) and prefix/KV cache priming so the runtime doesn't have to rebuild KV for hot sessions.
[01:52] Rachael Ortiz: Can you explain KV priming? We saw references to 'prefix caching' in the docs but not sure how it fits our chat flows.
[02:01] Diego Ramirez: Sure. Prefix caching means we keep a warmed KV state for common prefixes — for example, authentication handshakes or common prompt starts. When the model receives a request with that prefix, we hit the KV cache and skip the expensive recompute. If your workload has a small set of repeated prefixes, this can drop p99 significantly.
[02:20] Ibrahim Khan: But what about cache hotkeys? We get uneven access patterns where one customer session pins a shard and evicts others.
[02:28] Diego Ramirez: That's classic hotspotting. We suggested sharded KV with adaptive eviction and a small local LRU on the edge. Also consider heavier quantization to reduce memory footprint so more keys fit in GPU memory. But quantisation — ahem — quantization can change execution characteristics.
[02:45] Samir Patel: Do we have numbers for quantization latency tradeoffs? We're using int8 for most models.
[02:51] Diego Ramirez: Short answer: int8 typically reduces per-token compute by ~20-35% on our runtime, but you can see increased variance during cold starts because kernel selection differs and fallback paths might trigger slower code. We saw a case where p99 got worse by 60ms during a cold wave even though median dropped.
[03:12] Lena Park: So we should expect better medians but watch p99 closely.
[03:15] Diego Ramirez: Exactly. One mitigation: staged rollout of quantized variants with canary traffic and automatic fallback to fp16 when tail rises above threshold.
[03:26] Rachael Ortiz: About batching — we have bursty RPS, should we prefer constant small batches or dynamic batching?
[03:32] Diego Ramirez: Dynamic batching is workload-aware; it balances throughput for cost efficiency. But for tail-sensitive endpoints, you can configure a small max batch size and a micro-batch timeout (e.g., 4ms) to cap queueing delay. Streaming has no batching delay but, again, is sensitive to network jitter.
[03:49] Samir Patel: Could we do hybrid? Like streaming for short token-length requests and batch for long-running ones?
[03:55] Diego Ramirez: Yes, routing by request shape is a smart pattern — short interactive queries get streaming on low-hop paths; heavy content generation goes to batch queues possibly on dedicated capacity.
[04:06] Maya Chen: On the network side, we've seen customers improve p99 by pinning inference traffic to single region pop and using edge proxies to terminate the stream locally.
[04:16] Anna Liu: Our security team is concerned about on-prem proxies and key management. How does Redwood handle KMS in private deployments?
[04:23] Maya Chen: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support local key wrapping. For private/on-prem we provide a customer-managed control plane option. I'll send the security docs after the call.
[04:34] Rachael Ortiz: Thanks — please include audit log examples.
[04:38] Diego Ramirez: Back to tail debugging — we recommend correlating request traces with runtime KPI: token loop times, kv-miss rate, batch queue time, and network RTT. We can instrument sampling at 1% to capture detailed traces.
[04:53] Samir Patel: How intrusive is that sampling?
[04:56] Diego Ramirez: Minimal overhead, it's mostly additional span annotations and temporary metrics retention.
[05:02] Lena Park: What about cold-cache storms after deploys? We sometimes do rolling restarts and then a p99 spike that lasts 10-15 minutes.
[05:10] Diego Ramirez: That's expected if many new instances boot and need to coldfill KV. Two mitigations: 1) pre-warm KV by replaying a subset of traffic or synthetic priming, 2) use a staggered rollout so not all instances are cold at once. Also set a heavier warm cache retention on critical shards.
[05:26] Maya Chen: We're also going to test a hybrid fallback: primary fast variant (quantized) + fallback to stable fp16 when p99 crosses threshold. We can automate that.
[05:35] Rachael Ortiz: Can you show the expected cost implications? Quantized reduces GPU time but adds complexity.
[05:40] Diego Ramirez: We'll run a cost/perf matrix in the benchmark. Rough back of envelope: int8 may cut compute minutes by 25% but if you need to double warm instances to keep p99 low, the benefit shrinks. We'll model that.
[05:54] Ibrahim Khan: Anything about serialization/kv marshalling? We saw some RPC overhead in our mesh.
[06:00] Diego Ramirez: Yes, small serializers and binary codec help; avoid round-trips by bundling KV lookups when possible. Also ensure keepalive and TCP tuning on peered links.
[06:12] Lena Park: We have a question — do you support multi-path routing so internal traffic can pick low-latency link?
[06:18] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing policies can route by latency SLO, cost, or region. For latency-sensitive traffic we prefer lowest-latency path and will provide autoscaling to keep headroom.
[06:31] Samir Patel: Let's talk about observability: what traces do you need from our side?
[06:36] Diego Ramirez: Request id propagation, span for model enqueue/dequeue, kv-hit/miss tags, batch size, node id, and RTT to next hop. If you can send sample logs during spikes that's ideal.
[06:48] Rachael Ortiz: We'll gather those.
[06:50] Maya Chen: Quick recap — action items: run benchmark in your VPC, share top request shapes, Rachael send topology, Diego gather flamegraphs. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff once we have the benchmark results.
[07:04] Lena Park: Sounds good. Anything else?
[07:06] Diego Ramirez: One last tip: if you have a small high-frequency prefix set (auth + header), prime those keys during deploy windows; it's low-effort, big impact on p99.
[07:17] Samir Patel: Got it. Thanks everyone.
[07:19] Maya Chen: Thanks all — I'll follow up with the spreadsheet and invite.
